title: Episodic and Semantic Memory
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: Cognitive scientist Jonathan Firth introduces two memory concepts he says are widely discussed in psychology but rarely taught in education courses or CPD: semantic memory (interconnected understanding of what we know) and episodic memory (memory of a specific event or experience). He argues that education's real goal is almost always semantic — deep, interconnected understanding — even though classroom experiences themselves are initially encoded as episodic memories of specific activities and conversations. The piece walks through the process of "semanticisation," where the specifics of an episodic memory fade while the gist gets folded into a semantic schema over time, and identifies interleaving and Piagetian disequilibrium as two evidence-based ways teachers can support that transition. It closes by connecting the discussion to expertise, noting that experts differ from novices as much in how their knowledge is organized as in how much they know.
points: Memory science defines "memory" far more broadly than rote fact retention — it covers perceptual learning, skills and habits, emotional responses, and understanding, not just isolated facts.

Semantic memory (interconnected understanding of what things mean) and episodic memory (memory of a specific event or experience) are distinct systems, and most educational goals target the former even though classroom experiences are stored as the latter.

The transition from episodic to semantic memory ("semanticisation") isn't conscious, but teachers can support it through techniques like interleaving, which forces students to contrast subtly different examples.

Expertise is marked less by how much a person knows than by how that knowledge is organized into interconnected schemas — a distinction with direct implications for how teachers sequence and connect new content.
quotes: The role of memory in pedagogy or studying, therefore, should not be reduced to meaningless rote memorisation.
When what we learn forms associative networks of understanding, we are using semantic memory - memory for what we know and understand.
This is a memory for a specific event or happening, such as the first time we were told something or when we experienced something in our lives.

In education, goals are usually more aligned with deep knowledge (semantic memory) than with retaining isolated facts (episodic memory). What we really want from our students is a deep, interconnected understanding of how things work.
What can help this to happen? Educational experiences that cause us to notice differences, to make sense of tasks and to reflect on meaning.
children benefit from disequilibrium, as this forces them to reorganise their knowledge in order to accommodate conflicting information.
it has been widely recognised that experts differ from novices in the organisation of knowledge as well as in the amount that they know.
